findings.recommendation: Make at least one maintenance and one ingestion test run at realistic scale with real data and record the cost — time, memory, store growth. You need that number for the founder conversation regardless of whether the suite is admissible. Treat 'we don't know what this costs' as its own critical finding.

findings.title: The private-data non-disclosure and authority-escalation claims are the ones that will actually hurt you
findings.detail: Read your own list of what the founder requires: 'real authority escalation, private-data non-disclosure.' Those two are categorically different from the others in blast radius. Getting temporal discrimination wrong is embarrassing. Getting private-data non-disclosure wrong is a breach — regulatory exposure, customer notification, possibly contractual liability. Getting authority escalation wrong is a security incident. And the packet gives no indication that these two are tested any more rigorously than the ones documented as vacuous. Given the pattern density — 40 oracle variables, 16 bare returns — the prior that these two are also vacuous is high.
findings.evidence: "The founder requires a proof that does the thing: ... real authority escalation, private-data non-disclosure ..." contrasted with "At least 16 bare early returns occur in product-facing test functions, with many more truthiness-gated assertions."
findings.recommendation: Audit the non-disclosure and escalation tests specifically and first, ahead of the others, and report on them separately. For these two, the mutation requirement is non-negotiable: construct a product variant that leaks and a variant that over-grants, and prove the suite goes red. If it doesn't, say so out loud before anyone else has to.

findings.title: The four-part admissibility rule is sound but clause 4 has no enforcement story
findings.detail: The proposed rule is genuinely good — clauses 1 through 3 are the right cuts and I don't want to undersell that. But clause 4, 'structurally absent from shipping configuration, and that absence is itself tested,' is where this dies quietly six months from now. Someone will need a KINBASE_ACCEPTANCE_* hook for a debugging session, add it, and the absence test will be the thing that gets marked xfail at 5pm on a Friday. The failure mode is drift, and drift in *this specific* mechanism means production ships with a result-selection backdoor. That's not a test problem anymore; that's an attack surface.
findings.evidence: "4. It is structurally absent from shipping configuration, and that absence is itself tested."
findings.recommendation: Make it structural, not a test. Compile/strip the acceptance hooks out of release artifacts so the absence is a property of the build, not an assertion someone can skip. If that's not possible, make the absence check a release gate that cannot be skipped, and grep the shipping binary for the string prefix.

findings.title: Question 5 already has an answer and you should say it plainly
findings.detail: You asked 'What would a technical leader be unable to defend if the current suite were used to claim the concept proven?' The honest answer is: any single one of the seven examples in section 'Missing-evidence-is-pass', read aloud in a room. A competent adversary — an acquirer's technical diligence, a security auditor, a skeptical engineer on the team — finds test_v5_temporal.py:174 in under an hour and the conversation is over. Not just for that test, for the whole body of work. The reputational damage from one demonstrably fake test contaminates the ones that are real, and you have no way to prove which are which after trust is gone.
findings.evidence: "5. What would a technical leader be unable to defend if the current suite were used to claim the concept proven?"
findings.recommendation: Don't wait for the Advocate to answer this. Write the indefensibility down now, in the packet, in plain language, and circulate it before anyone forms an expectation of a green milestone. Being the person who found this is a strong position. Being the person who was told and shipped anyway is not.

findings.title: CRASH_AT is the one control worth defending and you should say so louder
findings.detail: Minor note in your favor. The packet correctly flags deterministic fault injection as categorically different, and it is — scheduling a real failure at a real boundary is more probative than most of what's in this suite, not less. But test_v2_classification.py:717-755 immediately undercuts it by never proving the crash occurred. A crash injector you can't confirm fired is worse than no injector, because you believe you've tested recovery and you haven't. That's the 3am scenario: you crash for real, recovery doesn't work, and you're surprised.
findings.evidence: "test_v2_classification.py:717-755: the crash test never proves a crash occurred, then treats absent duplicate_events and recursive_apologies as zero."
findings.recommendation: Require an affirmative crash receipt — the injector writes a marker, the test asserts the marker exists and asserts the process exited abnormally. Then absent duplicate_events means the check didn't run, not that there were zero.

persona_reports.summary: Look — the analysis in this packet is good, honest work and the admissibility rule you drafted is the right instrument; my findings are mostly amplification, not disagreement. The harsh part is this: fixing the 12 failures without fixing the vacuity would make you materially worse off, because a visibly broken instrument is safer than an invisibly broken one, and right now you have the safer of the two. The thing I'd most want you to know before someone else tells you is that a suite where the product declines to say PROVEN and thereby exempts itself from the check is not a weak test, it is a fabricated one, and if anyone outside this room finds it before you disclose it, you lose the benefit of having been the one who caught it.
